facts.title: Unified Static-Dynamic Pruning for Efficient LLM Inference
facts.event_hint: PVLDB 2026 paper (Seoul National University, arXiv:2607.21985v1) introduces SPDP, a unified static+dynamic weight-pruning GPU kernel framework for LLM decode/prefill inference.
facts.problem: LLM autoregressive decoding is memory-/bandwidth-bound, and existing weight-pruning systems are either purely static (fixed offline patterns, no input adaptivity) or purely dynamic (coarse-grained structured masks, hardware-incompatible, cannot exploit unstructured sparsity). Static-sparse kernels are row-major SpMM-optimized while dynamic pruning induces column-wise spMspV workloads, so the two are not directly composable: naively combining them breaks memory coalescing, warp stride regularity, and Tensor Core utilization.
facts.mechanism: SPDP co-designs a Tiled-Column-wise Bitmap Compressed (Tiled-CBC) weight layout with two kernels: (1) a CUDA-core spMspV decode kernel using Hybrid Activation-aware Dynamic Shared-Memory Bitmap Decoding (HAD-SMBD) for fine-grained runtime activation skipping, and (2) a Tensor-Core SpMM kernel for prefill that reuses the same layout via shared-memory alignment. Key insight: static pruning removes weights row-wise and dynamic pruning skips activations column-wise, acting on orthogonal dimensions, so their sparsity patterns overlap minimally and effective sparsities multiply. A roofline model (Section 3.2.3) formalizes this: CI_SPDP = M*N / (M/(CR*(1-s)) + N), where SP raises the compression ratio CR and DP cuts active columns by (1-s), so the two boost compute intensity multiplicatively in the memory-bound regime. The motivation for the co-design is the hardware-level conflict that under PTX mma.m16n8k16 a DP-induced spMspV drops Tensor-Core CI by up to 8x (achievable GEMV throughput ~one-fourth of CUDA-core FP32 peak), so a naive SP format would decode inactive fragments and fall below dense cuBLAS. The decode pipeline uses metadata-first prefetching (cp.async/LDGSTS.128, 128-bit vectors) and Split-K tiling (TILE_M=256, TILE_K=16) to hide HAD-SMBD latency; the prefill SpMM kernel adds a Layout Alignment stage for Tensor-Core execution.

evidence.claim: SPDP-spMspV kernel on A10G averages 1.24x speedup over SpInfer and 1.88x over cuBLAS (maxima 1.70x and 3.32x).
evidence.value: 1.24x avg / 1.70x max over SpInfer; 1.88x avg / 3.32x max over cuBLAS
evidence.baseline: SpInfer (SOTA Tensor-Core sparse kernel) and cuBLAS dense Tensor-Core baseline
evidence.condition: A10G GPU; static sparsity swept 0-90% with DP fixed at 30%; matrix shapes from OPT/LLaMA-2/3/Qwen/Qwen2/Mixtral/Phi/gpt-oss
evidence.source_locator: Section 5.4, Figure 8a (PDF Page 10)

evidence.claim: On L4 GPU, SPDP-spMspV averages 1.37x over SpInfer (max 2.52x) and 2.11x over cuBLAS (max 3.52x).
evidence.value: 1.37x avg / 2.52x max over SpInfer; 2.11x avg / 3.52x max over cuBLAS
evidence.condition: L4 GPU; DP fixed at 30%; same matrix-shape suite as A10G
evidence.source_locator: Section 5.4, Figure 8b (PDF Page 10)

evidence.claim: End-to-end decode TPOT speedup averages 1.34x over SpInfer at moderate sparsity on Llama-2-7B-hf while keeping perplexity under 5.4.
evidence.condition: Llama-2-7B-hf; A10G/L4/L40S; total sparsity up to 65% (best config 30% SP + 50% DP); full decode latency incl. attention/norm
evidence.source_locator: Section 5.5, Figure 11 (PDF Page 11)

evidence.claim: At matched perplexity, SPDP sustains up to 25% higher total sparsity than SpInfer (Wanda-based static pruning) with comparable or lower TPOT.
evidence.value: up to 25% higher total sparsity at matched PPL
evidence.condition: Matched perplexity (~4.97-5.34); A10G, L4, L40S GPUs
evidence.source_locator: Section 5.5, Figure 10 (PDF Page 11)

evidence.claim: SPDP-spMspV at (DP,SP)=(30%,30%) attains the highest SM-busy fraction and the lowest bank conflicts (74) versus SpInfer(30%) and SpInfer(50%) on A10G, with comparable Max bandwidth.
evidence.baseline: SpInfer at SP=30% and SP=50% (same total sparsity)
evidence.condition: A10G GPU; (DP,SP)=(30%,30%); metrics normalized to per-kernel peak
evidence.source_locator: Section 5.4, Figure 9 (PDF Page 11)

facts.evaluation_context: Inference-optimized GPUs: A10G, L4, L40S. Kernel benchmarks use projection/FFN weight-matrix shapes from OPT(13B-175B), LLaMA-2(7B-70B), LLaMA-3(8B/70B), Qwen(7B/14B), Qwen2(7B/72B), Mixtral-8x7B MoE, Phi-2/3, gpt-oss(20B/120B). End-to-end decode run on Llama-2-7B-hf. Practical sparsity range 30-50% for both SP and DP. Baselines: cuBLAS (dense), cuSPARSE, Sputnik, SparTA, Flash-LLM, SpInfer. The roofline analysis (Section 3.2.3) treats decode as memory-bound and expresses the SP+DP gain as a compute-intensity multiplier, not a measured energy metric.
facts.limitations: End-to-end gains are Amdahl-limited: attention, normalization and other non-sparse components are not sparsity-sensitive, and decode is memory-bound so higher sparsity improves arithmetic efficiency more than latency. Perplexity diverges sharply beyond ~70% static sparsity (Wanda impractical there). Quantization and unstructured sparsity do not compress multiplicatively in practice (low-bit reduces only Values; Bitmap, ColInfo, TileOffset and padding metadata persist). SPDP targets moderate-sparsity LLM decode; extreme-sparsity matrices (e.g., SuiteSparse) and large-N prefill (where existing works fail to beat cuBLAS) are out of scope. The targeted supplement (PDF Pages 5 and 8: roofline model, realization challenges, kernel pipeline and prefill SpMM design) provides no quantitative performance-per-watt/energy measurement and no prefill-stage Figure 12 speedup numbers, so the abstract's perf-per-watt claim and the prefill-kernel speedup remain un-located/un-quantified.
facts.project_relevance: Falls in the serving/runtime/compiler direction: SPDP is a projection-matmul kernel replacement for LLM serving engines, orthogonal to attention and compatible with continuous batching / fused prefill-decode. For our briefing it is a horizontal kernel-level sparse-inference observation, not a deployed at-scale system; the operationally meaningful number is the 1.34x end-to-end TPOT gain (and up to 25% extra sparsity at iso-quality), not the kernel-level 1.24-1.37x headline.
source_notes: The abstract headline '1.24x-1.37x average speedup (up to 2.51x)' corresponds to kernel-level spMspV measurements over SpInfer on A10G/L4 (Section 5.4, Figure 8); the end-to-end TPOT speedup is lower, averaging 1.34x (Section 5.5).
Artifacts at https://github.com/AIDASLab/SPDP; published as PVLDB 19(11) 2026.
Evidence pack covers abstract, intro, kernel profiling (Fig 8/9) and end-to-end eval (Fig 10/11); prefill kernel (Fig 12) and SuiteSparse (Fig 13) figures referenced but only qualitatively described.

Repair supplement (PDF Pages 5, 8) added the Section 3.2.3 roofline CI model, the Section 3.3 realization challenges (8x Tensor-Core CI drop under mma.m16n8k16), and the Section 4.2-4.3 kernel pipeline / prefill-SpMM design; it did NOT surface any energy/perf-per-watt data or Figure 12 prefill speedup numbers.

evidence_gaps.question: Does SPDP report a concrete performance-per-watt or energy measurement (watts/joules) backing the abstract's perf-per-watt claim, or is it only argued qualitatively?
What prefill-stage speedup does the Tensor-Core SpMM kernel achieve over cuBLAS and SpInfer (Figure 12 is referenced but no numbers given in the visible evidence)?

facts.title: CodeGrep: An RL-Trained Retrieval Agent for LLM Coding Agents
facts.event_hint: A 14B RL-trained agent-style code retriever (CodeGrep) that emits multi-turn parallel grep/glob/read calls and feeds candidate files to a frozen OpenHands agent, cutting rounds and tokens on SWE-Bench Verified while slightly lifting resolve rate.
facts.problem: LLM coding agents (Claude Code, OpenHands) spend most of their token budget finding the file to patch rather than patching it. On SWE-Bench Verified a 30B OpenHands agent averages 23 rounds and 631K tokens per resolved issue, dominated by grep/glob/view_file calls in ambiguous exploration loops, often 20+ rounds in a wrong direction before giving up. No open, systematically-studied agent-style code retriever exists at scale to shorten this phase.
facts.mechanism: CodeGrep is a 14B-parameter retriever built on Qwen3-14B-Instruct, trained end-to-end with GRPO in a custom Git-worktree RL environment. It exposes three read-only primitives (grep regex search, glob path matching, read file contents), emitting up to 8 concurrent tool calls per turn and up to 4 turns (3 exploration + 1 answer). Candidate files are injected into the prompt of a frozen, untouched OpenHands downstream agent, so any downstream effect is unambiguously attributable to the retriever. Supervision is mined via CATM from 67K open-source OpenHands trajectories (one-to-many attribution). A reward-design study (v1->v2->v3) shows that applying the efficiency signal at the advantage layer rather than the reward layer holds KL drift to roughly one-third, and that dropping an auxiliary line-range component improves both stability and downstream efficiency.

evidence.claim: On all 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances, CodeGrep v3 lifts resolve rate by +1.2pp (25.8%->27.0%) while cutting resolved rounds 23.0->19.6 (-15%) and resolved tokens 631K->514K (-19%) versus the no-retrieval OpenHands baseline. Section 5.3 caveat: these headline numbers are pooled over each configuration's OWN resolved set (baseline 129, v3 135) and therefore mix a genuine efficiency effect with a selection effect; on the 96 paired instances both configurations resolve, rounds fall 20.1->18.3 (-9%) and tokens 525K->448K (-15%), preserving 60-80% of the pooled effect and confirming the improvement as per-issue acceleration rather than a selection artifact.
evidence.value: 27.0% resolve; pooled -15% rounds/-19% tokens; paired -9% rounds/-15% tokens on 96 co-resolved
evidence.baseline: No-retrieval OpenHands + Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507: 25.8% resolve, 23.0 rounds, 631K tokens per resolved instance
evidence.condition: 500 SWE-Bench Verified instances; pooled accounting over each config's own resolved set; paired-instance accounting restricted to 96 co-resolved instances; frozen downstream agent
evidence.source_locator: Section 4.3 / Table 3 (PDF Page 6); Section 5.3 'Pooled vs. paired-instance efficiency' (PDF Page 8)

evidence.claim: Downstream utility follows a precision threshold across three retrievers: BM25 (file-precision 0.375) degrades the agent (resolve -0.6pp, resolved tokens +21%, 631K->763K); Jina (0.445) is neutral (resolve identical to baseline 25.8%, tokens -7%); only CodeGrep (0.677) crosses the threshold at which retrieval buys efficiency.
evidence.value: BM25 0.375 hurts; Jina 0.445 neutral; CodeGrep 0.677 helps
evidence.condition: Injected into the same frozen OpenHands + Qwen3-30B-A3B agent
evidence.source_locator: Section 5.1 and Section 4.3, PDF Page 6; precision figures from Table 2

evidence.claim: Intrinsic retrieval quality (Table 2): CodeGrep v3 reaches file-precision 0.677, recall 0.435, F-beta mean 0.576, 43.0% of cases at F-beta>=0.8, in 2.3 agentic turns, versus BM25 (precision 0.375, recall 0.386, 7.0% F-beta>=0.8) and Jina-1.5B (precision 0.445, recall 0.468, 7.0%).
evidence.value: CodeGrep v3 precision 0.677 / recall 0.435 / 43.0% F-beta>=0.8 / 2.3 turns
evidence.condition: Internal evaluation set; turns column applies only to the agentic retriever
evidence.source_locator: Table 2, PDF Page 6

evidence.claim: Reward-design study: reward-layer multiplicative scaling of a tool-call penalty (v1) drives KL-to-reference to ~0.31 by step 900, while advantage-layer scaling (v2/v3) holds KL at 0.09/0.15 (~one-third); v3 also converges higher on reward (0.60-0.65 vs 0.45-0.48 for v1/v2) and stabilizes tool-use turns at ~2.1 vs rebound to ~2.6 for v1/v2. Removing the auxiliary line-range term (F_beta^lr) eliminates a signal with no downstream consumer (the editor takes no line ranges) and is systematically zero on CATM-only entries.
evidence.condition: Same ~900-step GRPO training run on 8xB200
evidence.source_locator: Section 3.5 and Figure 2, PDF Pages 2 and 5; Table 1, PDF Page 5; v3 discussion Section 5.2, PDF Page 8

evidence.claim: Engineering scale: supervision mined from 67,074 raw OpenHands trajectories, filtered by a GLM-5.1-FP8 judge (16-way parallel, thresholds reasoning_tokens>=30 and w>=0.15) to 31,977 effective training samples (47.7% retention); training runs on a single 8xB200 node for ~27 hours wall-clock, early-stopped at step 897 of a planned 2000-step budget.
evidence.value: 31,977 effective samples (47.7% retention); 27h on 8xB200; stop at step 897/2000
evidence.condition: LoRA + optimizer offload + vLLM-colocated rollout on ms-swift; CATM pipeline
evidence.source_locator: Section 3.6 PDF Page 5; Table 5 PDF Page 12

facts.evaluation_context: Benchmark: SWE-Bench Verified (all 500 instances). Downstream agent: OpenHands with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, temperature 0, 100-round max; no-retrieval baseline 25.8% resolve / 23.0 rounds / 631K tokens per resolved issue (within one SD of publicly reported 25.2+-0.7%). Retriever: CodeGrep 14B built on Qwen3-14B-Instruct. Six configurations compared (baseline, BM25, Jina-1.5B, CodeGrep v1/v2/v3). Training hardware: single 8xB200 node, LoRA, ~27h. RL environment uses Git worktrees with up to 8 concurrent tool calls/turn, max 4 turns, tool-concurrency cap 64 (asyncio semaphore), max 32 tool execs per rollout. Efficiency accounting (Sec 5.3): headline Table 3 numbers are pooled per-config over its own resolved set (baseline 129, v3 135) and thus mix efficiency with a selection effect; a paired analysis on the 96 co-resolved instances preserves 60-80% of the pooled effect (-9% rounds, -15% tokens), confirming per-issue acceleration. A representative action-level trace (Sec 6, django-15278) shows injection converting a stalled 74-action/3.2M-token rollout with no patch into a 15-action/307K-token success (~10x fewer tokens).
facts.limitations: Only one downstream agent stack is evaluated (OpenHands + Qwen3-30B-A3B), so generalization to Claude Code, Cursor, or Windsurf is untested. The benefit of dropping the line-range reward term is conjectured to be editor-interface dependent: agents whose editor consumes full files (OpenHands, Cursor) benefit, while agents whose editor consumes line ranges (plausibly Windsurf Cascade) may not. v1 matches v3's resolve rate (27.0%) but not its efficiency (-1.3% rounds, -0.6% tokens, essentially flat), showing resolve rate alone does not predict efficiency. The headline -15%/-19% efficiency figures are pooled and partly reflect a selection effect (v3 resolves 6 more instances than baseline); the paired -9%/-15% on co-resolved instances is the conservative estimate. Comparison to concurrent Cognition SWE-grep is necessarily partial because their reward formulation is not fully disclosed. Inference-time wall-clock latency is not reported; efficiency is measured only via rounds and tokens. CodeGrep's contribution is concentrated on rollout cost, not resolve rate (Sec 7).
facts.project_relevance: Directly targets the agent-acceleration problem of repeated grep/glob/read exploration: it gives an open, trainable retriever that shortens the file-finding phase and reports the exact metrics the topic values (rounds, tokens, tool-call counts, resolve rate). The precision-threshold characterization (hurts/neutral/buys efficiency) is a portable design heuristic for deciding when retrieval injection into a coding agent will pay off. The advantage-layer (vs reward-layer) efficiency-scaling result is a transferable RL-training insight for any tool-policy reward mixing accuracy with efficiency. For a code-agent optimization path (search symbol -> read file -> locate call chain -> patch -> verify), this validates front-loading retrieval into a specialized submodule; the §5.3 paired accounting and §6 action trace show the savings come from compressing the exploratory prefix of repo-wide find/grep sweeps, not from supplying the fix.
source_notes: Primary source: arXiv 2608.05886v1 (fetched, FETCHED). Evidence Pack covers PDF Pages 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 (abstract, intro, related work, method 3.1-3.6, experiments 4.1-4.3, analysis 5.1-5.3, case study 6, limitations 7, appendix Table 5).
Resolve-rate and efficiency headline numbers in the abstract are corroborated by Table 3 / Section 4.3 with full baselines, so they are treated as verified experiment facts, not unverified claims.

Section 5.3 (PDF Page 8) qualifies the headline efficiency: pooled -15% rounds/-19% tokens mix a selection effect (baseline 129 vs v3 135 resolved); paired on 96 co-resolved instances the effect is -9% rounds/-15% tokens (60-80% of pooled).

Section 6 case study (django-15278, PDF Page 8): baseline 74 actions/3.2M tokens/no patch -> injection 15 actions/307K tokens/patch passes; CodeGrep compresses exploratory find/grep prefix, does not supply the fix itself.
Authors plan to release model, CATM pipeline, RL environment, and evaluation harnesses.

facts.title: TensorCast: The Missing Tensor Management Layer in Large Language Model Infrastructure
facts.event_hint: arXiv preprint (2608.06007v1, 6 Aug 2026) proposing TensorCast / Tensor-as-a-Service (TaaS), a distributed tensor lifecycle management layer for LLM infrastructure, integrated with vLLM and SGLang.
facts.problem: Existing LLM systems optimize individual tensor management tasks (weight loading, KV cache placement/transfer, checkpoint sync) by deeply coupling task-specific mechanisms with execution engines, networks, or storage backends, creating isolated silos that prevent reuse/composition and block cross-component optimizations such as jointly balancing instance load and KV cache locality.
facts.mechanism: A Tensor-as-a-Service (TaaS) layer decouples tensor lifecycle management from computation: first-class tensor abstractions (system-owned Artifact, caller-leased tensors), programmable lifecycle primitives (identify/place/materialize/transform_into/coordinate), a distributed tensor pool plus lifecycle runtime that separates policies from execution mechanisms, and an instance adaptor that confines engine-specific import/export. Uses view() for rank-specific slicing/resharding, CUDA IPC zero-copy for warm materialization (vLLM consumes pre-materialized tensors via tensor_dict in under 1 second), and a userspace mTCP implementation with multipath transmission for non-RDMA KV transfer.

evidence.claim: TensorCast accelerates large-tensor materialization in two scenarios. (a) Model weight synchronization (RL training-serving sync): 1.61x-2.00x for Qwen3-14B and 1.14x-2.63x for Qwen3-32B vs the Default JFS updater across TP=1/2/4 (Fig. 7). (b) MaaS instance launch (single-node, 8xH800, TP=8, safetensors from JuiceFS/SSD/tmpfs): under JFS for Qwen3-30B-A3B, TensorCast-cold cuts weight-load time by 60.7x vs Default and 10.2x vs InstantTensor, and end-to-end launch-ready time by 28.5x and 5.4x; TensorCast-warm (CUDA IPC prefetch) consumes weights in <1s, yielding 228.6x and 40.7x end-to-end launch speedups over Default and InstantTensor for Qwen3-235B-A22B (Fig. 5/6).
evidence.value: sync 1.14x-2.63x; launch cold 60.7x/10.2x load & 28.5x/5.4x ready; launch warm 228.6x/40.7x ready
evidence.baseline: Default (native vLLM loader / JFS updater) and InstantTensor fast weight loader
evidence.condition: Sync: 2-node, 64 CPU, 500GB DRAM, 4xH800, RDMA disabled for fairness, Qwen3-14B/32B. Launch: single node, 64 CPU, 500GB DRAM, 8xH800, vLLM TP=8, weights in safetensors from JuiceFS / node-local SSD / tmpfs.
evidence.source_locator: Sec 6.1 Setup/Results + Fig 5/6 (instance launch) and Sec 6.2 + Fig 7 (weight sync), PDF Page 11-12

evidence.claim: For Qwen3-32B (TP=2) KV cache retrieval, with RDMA enabled TensorCast achieves TTFT reductions of 60% to 87.5% (2.5x to 8x speedup) comparable to Mooncake, and significantly outperforms Mooncake with RDMA disabled.
evidence.value: 60% to 87.5% TTFT reduction (2.5x-8x speedup) with RDMA
evidence.baseline: State-of-the-art Mooncake KV-centric integration in SGLang under identical settings
evidence.condition: N-node cluster; each node 64 CPU, 1 TB DRAM, 8 x H800 GPUs, 200 Gbps RDMA links; LongBench prompts (~16k and ~35k tokens); 100% cache-hit rate stress test; TTFT reduction measured for N-1 instances relative to first instance.
evidence.source_locator: Section 6.3 'High-Cardinality Tensor Management', Results paragraph (Fig. 8a-8d), PDF Page 12-13.

evidence.claim: For Qwen3-235B-A22B (TP=8), TensorCast is comparable to Mooncake under RDMA and better without RDMA; TP=8 introduces 4x more concurrent KV page retrieval requests than TP=2, increasing contention and reducing TTFT improvements for both systems.
evidence.baseline: Mooncake KV storage backend in SGLang
evidence.condition: Same N-node H800 cluster; TP=8; 16k/35k token prompts; Fig. 9a-9d.
evidence.source_locator: Section 6.3, Results (Fig. 9), PDF Page 13.

evidence.claim: A programmable request-routing policy implemented with TensorCast (cache-aware routing plus KV-cache-migrating load rebalancing) improves median TTFT by up to 93.2% under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads.
evidence.baseline: Compared against Load-aware, Load-aware+Mooncake, and Cache-aware router policies (Fig. 10)
evidence.condition: Highly concurrent multi-turn agentic coding workloads; three LogNorm inter-turn delay presets (fast/medium/slow, Table 3); exact comparison cell and session count not restated in visible text.
evidence.source_locator: Abstract (PDF Page 1); Section 6.4 'Programmable Request Router' and Fig. 10/11 (PDF Page 13-14).

evidence.claim: Agent workload presets use LogNorm-sampled inter-turn delays: fast (median 8.2s, P95 22.0s), medium (median 20.1s, P95 75.0s), slow (median 60.3s, P95 311s), representing tight coding-agent loops, typical SWE agents, and long research/planning agents respectively.
evidence.condition: Synthetic LogNorm sampling within a session used to drive the §6.4 router evaluation.
evidence.source_locator: Table 3 'The three inter-turn delay presets used by the LogNorm sampling within a session', PDF Page 13.

facts.evaluation_context: Hardware: 2-node and N-node clusters of H800 GPUs (4x or 8x per node), 64 CPUs, 500 GB-1 TB DRAM, 200 Gbps RDMA links; the instance-launch study (Sec 6.1) uses a single 8xH800 node (TP=8) with weights in safetensors from JuiceFS / node-local SSD / tmpfs. Baselines: Default JFS weight updater, InstantTensor fast loader, and Mooncake (SGLang KV backend). Models: Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-235B-A22B with TP=1/2/4/8. Datasets/workloads: LongBench prompts (~16k/35k tokens), 100% cache-hit KV-reuse stress test, MaaS instance-launch (cold/warm materialization), and simulated multi-turn agent sessions (LogNorm inter-turn delays). Integrations: vLLM and SGLang. Reported metrics are TTFT reduction ratios, weight-sync/launch speedups, and cache-hit rate vs session count; absolute TPOT, token throughput, end-to-end P95 TTFT, and network utilization are not reported.
facts.limitations: Evaluations cover inference workloads only; training-framework integration (Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed) is explicitly left as future work (Discussion, PDF Page 14). Authors explicitly disclaim that a general abstraction is inherently faster than every specialized implementation; under RDMA, TensorCast is only comparable (not superior) to Mooncake, with its advantage concentrated in the non-RDMA and composability cases. The headline 93.2% TTFT gain is conditioned on highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads and a specific programmable policy; the exact comparison baseline and session count are not restated in the visible text, and the targeted supplement (Sec 6.1 instance launch) did not expose the §6.4 router detail either. The deployment-level metrics requested (absolute TPOT, token throughput, end-to-end P95 TTFT, network utilization) are still absent. Agent workloads use synthetic LogNorm-sampled delays rather than a production trace. This is an arXiv v1 preprint.
facts.project_relevance: Relevant to the KV-cache-aware network/scheduling question: TensorCast provides a composable layer where request routing, KV placement, and instance load can be jointly programmed, and it reports TTFT reductions and a 93.2% median-TTFT agent-workload gain. However, the visible evidence reports reduction ratios rather than absolute TPOT, token throughput, end-to-end P95, or network utilization, and the network-side value is mainly in the non-RDMA (mTCP multipath) and cross-component composition cases rather than beating specialized RDMA KV systems head-to-head. Treat as a systems/preprint signal on composability, pending absolute tail metrics and training-side validation.

facts.title: SAC: Disaggregated KV Cache System for Sparse Attention LLMs with CXL
facts.event_hint: SAC (arXiv 2606.19746v1) is presented as the first CXL-based disaggregated KV cache system for sparse-attention LLMs, fetching only the dynamically selected top-k KV entries on demand at cache-line granularity via CXL load/store, instead of RDMA full-prefix fetch.
facts.problem: RDMA-based disaggregated KV cache systems fetch the entire prefix KV cache into local memory before decoding (coarse-grained). For sparse-attention models where only a small top-k subset of KV is active per layer, this causes two problems: (P1) transmission bottleneck over RDMA, and (P2) local memory wasting, since the bulk of the fetched KV is never used during decode yet must be held locally, forcing TB-level local memory for high concurrency.
facts.mechanism: SAC keeps the full KV cache in a disaggregated CXL memory pool (multiple CXL-MEM devices behind a CXL switch, host GPUs on PCIe 5.0 x16 / 64 GB/s links). The decode instance (built on the HiSparse framework in SGLang) computes the per-layer top-k selection at runtime and, during each attention layer, directly fetches only those top-k KV entries from the CXL pool into GPU HBM using CXL cache-line-granularity load/store semantics with near-DRAM latency; newly generated token KV is written back to the CXL pool. Three components: a Prefill Instance (writes full KV to the pool), a Decode Instance (on-demand top-k fetch), and a CXL-based KV cache manager exposing a global CXL address space with optimized read/write kernels and device interleaving. The HiSparse device_buffer_size (4K vs 6K) controls the GPU HBM hot-KV cache capacity and thus the CXL fetch volume.

evidence.claim: On DeepSeek-V3.2 (AWQ 4-bit quantization) served via SGLang+HiSparse on an 8xH20 GPU server with a 2TB CXL memory pool, SAC achieves on average 2.1x higher throughput, 9.7x lower TTFT, and 1.8x lower TBT than an RDMA-based memory pool. These are Round-2 (cache-hit / decode-only) results; RDMA's high TTFT stems from transmission-bandwidth saturation under client concurrency and its 1.8x TBT from PCIe bus contention between KV traffic and the HiSparse swap-in process.
evidence.value: 2.1x throughput / 9.7x lower TTFT / 1.8x lower TBT vs RDMA pool
evidence.condition: DeepSeek-V3.2 AWQ 4-bit; 8xH20 server; 2TB CXL pool; SGLang + HiSparse; Round-2 (cache hit), 512 ShareGPT requests, concurrency 64, context 16K-128K, output 1K tokens; confirmed in Evaluation Sec 5.1
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7, Sec 5.1 (End-to-End Performance Comparison), Figures 9-10

evidence.claim: Against a local-host-DRAM upper bound on the same workload, SAC achieves throughput within 91% of the DRAM baseline (i.e. ~9% degradation) on average, with only marginal TBT and TTFT increases, supporting the near-optimal claim for CXL disaggregation.
evidence.condition: DeepSeek-V3.2 AWQ 4-bit; 8xH20; Round-1 + Round-2; confirmed in Evaluation Sec 5.1
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 7, Sec 5.1

evidence.claim: Sparse KV retrieval-latency microbenchmark (DRAM vs CXL vs RDMA): at 2048 fetched KV indices CXL is ~1.63x DRAM while RDMA is ~19.7x DRAM, with the RDMA/DRAM gap widening as the fetched-index count grows (3.97x at 64 indices up to 19.7x at 2048).
evidence.value: CXL ~1.63x / RDMA ~19.7x relative to DRAM at 2048 indices
evidence.condition: Per-index sparse KV read latency microbenchmark; absolute latency values not given in the figure
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 4, Figure 5 (Retrieval latency comparison for sparse KV)

evidence.claim: KV cache footprint and utilization for DeepSeek-V3.2 (ShareGPT, 1K-token output): per-request footprint is 1.2/2.3/4.6/9.2 GB at 16K/32K/64K/128K context, and at 128K only ~21% of the KV cache is actually utilized, quantifying the local-memory-wasting problem.
evidence.condition: DeepSeek-V3.2; ShareGPT dataset; 1K-token output; profiling of active vs inactive KV
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 4, Figure 4 (KV cache usage and footprint for DeepSeek-V3.2)

evidence.claim: RDMA prefix-KV prefetch latency under a 100 Gbps RNIC grows near-linearly with concurrency and context length, reaching dozens of seconds in high-concurrency scenarios and directly inflating TTFT.
evidence.value: dozens of seconds at high concurrency
evidence.condition: Average KV-cache transmission latency across concurrency 1-32 and contexts 16K-128K
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 4, Figure 3 (RDMA prefetch latency for prefix KV cache)

facts.evaluation_context: Model: DeepSeek-V3.2 (AWQ 4-bit quantization; native sparse attention, DSA, top-k=2048 KV latent vectors). Hardware: 8xH20 GPU server with a 2TB CXL memory pool as KV cache backend. Serving stack: SGLang integrated with the HiSparse framework. Workload: 512 requests sampled from ShareGPT; context lengths swept 16K-128K; output length fixed at 1K tokens. Two-round setup: Round-1 (Cache Populate, prefill instance, concurrency 8) and Round-2 (Cache Hit, decode instance, prefill bypassed, concurrency 64). Baselines: RDMA-based memory pool and local host DRAM as upper bound. Headline 2.1x/9.7x/1.8x are Round-2 (decode) results; SAC reaches ~91% of DRAM throughput. Device-interleaving across CXL devices mitigates link contention and the HiSparse device_buffer_size (6K vs 4K) yields ~10.4% higher average throughput via a lower KV miss rate. The exact CXL device count, per-device CXL latency, and the specific RDMA baseline implementation/RNIC model are still not named in the read sections.
facts.limitations: Applicability is restricted to sparse-attention models (DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5.1, DeepSeek-V4 cited); dense-attention models are out of scope (existing CXL work Beluga/TRACT does full-prefix prefetch for dense models). Top-k is fixed at 2048 in the current DSA implementation. The 3x throughput / 256-concurrency / 8xH200 GLM-5.1-FP8 result in Appendix C is HiSparse's prior-work basis, not SAC's own end-to-end result. The headline numbers are now validated in the detailed Evaluation (Sec 5.1) with hardware (8xH20, 2TB CXL pool, AWQ 4-bit) and concurrency (Round-1=8, Round-2=64) known; however the exact CXL device count/per-device latency, the named RDMA baseline (MoonCake/LMCache/RNIC model), and Appendix A setup details remain unread. Source is an arXiv preprint (v1, 2026-06-18).
facts.project_relevance: Directly addresses the topic's memory-semantics question: SAC demonstrates that CXL cache-line-granularity load/store (vs RDMA message-passing) changes remote memory placement/sharing semantics enough to enable fine-grained, on-demand sparse KV access. It also shows end-to-end propagation of a memory-tier change to LLM serving metrics (throughput, TTFT, TBT on SGLang + DeepSeek-V3.2), which is exactly the 'does the benefit reach end-to-end' question on the project card. Note: the offload here is GPU<->CXL-memory data movement via CXL, not Intel DSA/IAA device offload, so it informs the CXL/disaggregated-memory half of the topic rather than the DSA/IAA卸载 half.

Keywords: CXL, disaggregated KV cache, sparse attention, DeepSeek-V3.2, SGLang, HiSparse, top-k KV, load/store semantics, RDMA pooling, TTFT/TBT/throughput.
DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) top-k = 2048 KV latent vectors per layer (PDF Page 3).
